openers.climate-finance-and-agreements: No country can stop climate change alone, so the world has tried to do it by treaty. At the center sits a UN convention whose stated goal is to keep greenhouse gases below the level that would dangerously disturb the climate. Each year its member countries meet at a conference to negotiate, and from those meetings came two landmark treaties, one in Kyoto and one in Paris. Under the second, every country writes its own pledge for cutting emissions and adapting. Behind every pledge sits a question of money: who pays to cut emissions, adapt and build resilience, and whether investors should pull their money out of fossil fuels.

reviews.climate-finance-and-agreements: The climate treaties moved from one design to another. Kyoto imposed binding cuts on industrialised countries only. Paris asks every country for its own pledge and relies on regular review to ratchet ambition up. Money runs through both: rich countries promised $100 billion a year, missed the date, and at COP29 agreed $300 billion a year by 2035, which poorer nations called insufficient. Arguments over fairness, from common but differentiated responsibilities to climate debt and reparations, shape every negotiation. Results so far are mixed: projected warming has fallen, yet most experts judge current pledges insufficient for 1.5 °C.

nature-clim-053.title: The UN climate convention: where the world negotiates
nature-clim-053.text: At the 1992 {{ref:nature-hist-003}} in Rio de Janeiro, 154 states signed a treaty on {{ref:nature-hist-007}}. The United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change, or UNFCCC, entered into force in 1994. It is both a treaty and the UN process built on it, through which countries negotiate how to limit dangerous climate change. Its ultimate aim, in Article 2, is to stabilise greenhouse gas concentrations at a level that prevents dangerous human interference with the climate system. It also set a principle of fairness, {{ref:nature-clim-084}}. Every country shares the duty, but developed countries are expected to lead because of their larger historical emissions. By 2022 the convention had 198 parties. Its supreme body, the Conference of the Parties, meets every year. Its work now centres on carrying out {{ref:nature-clim-074}}, which entered into force in 2016. Decisions are taken by consensus, so any party can block them. That has a cost. The convention has been criticised as unsuccessful at cutting emissions.

nature-clim-042.title: Climate finance: following the money
nature-clim-042.text: Global climate finance was estimated at around $1.3 trillion per year in 2021/2022, up from more than US$600 billion in 2019 by one estimate. Climate finance is money used to cut greenhouse gas emissions, adapt to climate change or build resilience. It can take the form of loans, grants or government budget spending. It can come from private or public sources, and can pass through intermediaries such as multilateral development banks, lenders owned by many governments, and development agencies. Under the UN Climate Convention the term is narrower. It means transfers of public money from high-income to low- and middle-income countries, in line with their duty to provide new and additional resources. It has two main parts. {{ref:nature-clim-043}} aims to reduce emissions, and {{ref:nature-clim-044}} responds to the consequences of climate change. Most of the money stays home: 84% in 2021/2022 was raised and spent within the same country. It is far from enough. A 2024 report estimated that flows must rise at least sixfold, to $8.5 trillion per year by 2030. Public budgets are widely seen as too small, so private finance is expected to matter for closing the gap. The main challenges are tracking the flows, supporting developing countries fairly and giving private investors suitable incentives.

nature-clim-094.title: The Montreal Protocol: the treaty that worked
nature-clim-094.text: Often called the most successful environmental treaty between nations, the Montreal Protocol protects the ozone layer by phasing out the production of substances that deplete it. It was agreed on 16 September 1987 and entered into force on 1 January 1989. With 198 parties, it was the first universally ratified treaty in UN history. It helped poorer members. Under Article 5 developing countries get extra time to comply, and a financial mechanism under Article 10 helps them pay. The results show. Concentrations of the main CFCs, ozone-destroying chemicals, have levelled off or fallen, and the Antarctic ozone hole is slowly recovering. The treaty also helped mitigation, because HCFCs, which it phases out, are very potent greenhouse gases. It is cited as a precedent that the UN consensus approach to global problems can work.

nature-clim-086.title: Fossil fuel divestment: pulling money out of oil and coal
nature-clim-086.text: It began on US university campuses in 2011. By 2015 fossil fuel divestment was reportedly the fastest-growing divestment movement in history. Divestment means pressuring institutions to sell their stocks, bonds and other investments in fossil fuel extraction companies, as a way to fight climate change. As of July 2023, more than 1593 institutions with over $40.5 trillion in assets had begun or committed to some form of it. Divesters have three kinds of reason: to align investments with values, to fight the fossil fuel industry, or to protect portfolios from climate-related financial risk. One financial motive is stranded assets, the 'carbon bubble': reserves that cannot be burned safely and would have to be written off. The aim is to speed the shift to renewable energy by stigmatising fossil fuel companies. Those companies have partly blamed divestment pressure for the rising cost of raising money.

nature-clim-100.title: The COPs: the yearly climate summits
nature-clim-100.text: Every year the parties to {{ref:nature-clim-053}} meet to assess and negotiate climate action. These meetings are the United Nations Climate Change Conferences, known as COPs. The first, COP 1, was held in Berlin in 1995. Since 2005 they also serve as the meeting of the parties to {{ref:nature-clim-056}}. From 2011 to 2015 they were used to negotiate {{ref:nature-clim-074}}. Any final text must be agreed by consensus. Hosting rotates among the five UN regional groups. Not everyone present is a negotiator. More than 5,350 fossil fuel industry lobbyists attended the four conferences from 2021 to 2024.

nature-clim-055.title: Annex I, Annex II and the rest: sorting countries by duty
nature-clim-055.text: The climate convention does not treat all countries alike. Since 1992 it has sorted them into groups with different duties. Annex I holds industrialised countries and economies in transition. There are 43 Annex I parties, including the EU. Fourteen of them are economies in transition, the former Soviet-bloc economies. Annex I countries should adopt national policies to limit their emissions and report on returning to their 1990 levels. Annex II is a smaller, richer group. Its 24 parties are OECD members, the club of wealthy market economies, and they must give financial and technical support to transition economies and developing countries. Everyone else, mostly developing countries, is non-Annex I. Among all parties, 49 are least-developed countries with special status. The lines can move. Developing countries may volunteer to join Annex I once sufficiently developed.

nature-clim-056.title: The Kyoto Protocol: binding cuts for rich countries
nature-clim-056.text: Adopted in Kyoto on 11 December 1997, the Kyoto Protocol extended {{ref:nature-clim-053}} with commitments to reduce {{ref:nature-eco-163}}. It entered into force on 16 February 2005. Its main feature was legally binding emission-cut commitments for Annex I, the industrialised parties described in {{ref:nature-clim-055}}. That followed the principle of {{ref:nature-clim-084}}. It covered seven gases, including carbon dioxide, methane and nitrous oxide. The first commitment period ran from 2008 to 2012. The 36 fully participating countries pledged a 4% combined cut from 1990 levels. They achieved emissions 24.2% below 1990 in 2008–2012. That success came largely from the Soviet Union's collapse and the 2008 financial crisis. Meanwhile global emissions rose by 32% from 1990 to 2010, because the committed countries made up only 24% of global emissions in 2010. The United States never ratified the treaty, and Canada withdrew effective December 2012. It was followed in 2015 by {{ref:nature-clim-074}}, a separate instrument under the convention, not an amendment.

nature-clim-074.title: The Paris Agreement: every country pledges
nature-clim-074.text: In 2015, 196 parties met near Paris for the UN climate conference and negotiated a new treaty. The Paris Agreement covers mitigation, adaptation and finance, and entered into force on 4 November 2016. It aims to keep warming well below 2 °C above pre-industrial levels and preferably to 1.5 °C, with emissions reaching net zero by mid-century. Its design breaks with {{ref:nature-clim-056}}. Each country sets its own contributions, and each new target should go beyond the last. Nothing forces a country to set a specific target. It also blurs the line between developed and developing countries, so developing countries must submit emission-cut plans too. The EU and 194 states, covering over 98% of greenhouse gas emissions, have ratified or joined it. The United States withdrew in 2020, rejoined in 2021 and withdrew again in 2026. The agreement recognises loss and damage as a separate pillar, but states that it cannot be used as a basis for liability. Global emissions kept rising after it was signed, and most experts say it is insufficient for its 1.5 °C goal.

nature-clim-071.title: Nationally determined contributions: each country's own pledge
nature-clim-071.text: At the heart of {{ref:nature-clim-074}} lies a simple idea: each country decides for itself what to contribute. A nationally determined contribution, or NDC, is a country's own pledge of how it will cut greenhouse gas emissions and adapt to climate change. NDCs must be renewed every five years, and each should be more ambitious than the last, a rule called the principle of progression. The legal force is limited. The pledges themselves are not binding, but preparing, communicating and updating them is. There is no way to force a country to meet its target. Some pledges are unconditional. Others depend on outside finance, technical support or other countries' ambition. NDCs are the first UNFCCC emission targets that apply equally to developed and developing countries. They still fall short. Emission cuts must rise 80% beyond current NDCs to likely meet 2 °C. On current trends, the chance of staying below 2 °C is only 5%.

nature-clim-066.title: Article 6: how countries can cooperate on their pledges
nature-clim-066.text: Article 6 is the part of the 2015 Paris Agreement that sets out how countries may cooperate voluntarily to carry out their {{ref:nature-clim-071}}. The aim is to allow higher ambition in mitigation and adaptation while promoting {{ref:nature-eecon-209}}. That depends on environmental integrity, transparency and robust accounting. There are three pathways: cooperative approaches that trade emission reductions between countries (6.2), a UN-supervised crediting mechanism (6.4) and cooperation without trading, {{ref:nature-clim-069}}. The core 'Article 6 rulebook' was adopted at COP26 in Glasgow in 2021. It succeeds the Kyoto Protocol's flexible mechanisms, with the transition expected to be completed by 2025. Its impact is debated. Some analysts say the transfers lower costs and mobilise finance. Others fear they undermine integrity through over-crediting, weak baselines and surplus allowances, {{ref:nature-clim-058}}.

nature-clim-054.title: The convention's ultimate goal: avoiding dangerous interference
nature-clim-054.text: Article 2 of {{ref:nature-clim-053}} sets its ultimate objective: stabilise greenhouse gas concentrations at a level that prevents dangerous human interference with the climate. It adds a speed limit. This should happen fast enough to let ecosystems adapt naturally, keep food production safe and let economic development continue sustainably. Stabilising concentrations requires global emissions to peak and then decline, and earlier for lower stabilisation levels. One word is hard. Science can describe climate risks, but deciding which risks count as dangerous needs value judgements. Article 3 acknowledges the precautionary principle, so uncertainty about climate effects is no reason for inaction.

nature-clim-083.title: Climate targets: goals set by politics and science
nature-clim-083.text: At least 164 countries have climate targets written into their national law. A climate target, also called a climate goal or pledge, is a measurable long-term commitment in climate and energy policy aimed at limiting climate change. Politicians set temperature targets based on research into the likely effects of different levels of warming. These targets underpin carbon budgets and emission targets. Under Kyoto, countries pledged an average 5.2 percent cut on 1990 levels over 2008 to 2012. An emissions target may differ from what science allows, because it can reflect what is politically palatable. Many targets lie above the scientifically allowable emissions. Many also rely on negative-emission technologies, ways of pulling carbon out of the air, that are not yet developed.

nature-clim-084.title: Common but differentiated responsibilities: a shared duty, unequally held
nature-clim-084.text: All countries share a duty to tackle environmental damage, but not to the same degree. That principle, common but differentiated responsibilities, was set in the 1992 UN climate convention. Developed countries industrialised earlier and contributed more to climate change, so they agreed to take greater responsibility for mitigation. Article 3 says they should take the lead. The principle can be read as a form of polluter pays, measuring responsibility by historical contribution and ability to act. Its meaning changed over time. Under Kyoto it meant a rigid split in which only industrialised countries had strict limits. Under Paris each country sets its own contribution as its circumstances change. It remains disputed. Critics, including US negotiators, argued it gave developing countries an unfair economic advantage. Developing countries replied that their emissions are for survival, while rich countries' are 'luxury emissions'.

nature-clim-044.title: Adaptation finance: the public money that keeps people safe
nature-clim-044.text: Adaptation finance is the part of {{ref:nature-clim-042}} that pays for responding to the consequences of climate change. It can come from governments, development finance institutions and {{ref:nature-clim-047}}, and from banks, investors, companies and households. In practice, around 98% of tracked adaptation finance has come from public sources. Adaptation projects rarely have a clear income stream or attractive return. Only around 4-8% of total climate finance has gone to adaptation. The benefits can be large: every US$1 billion invested against coastal flooding is estimated to cut economic damages by US$14 billion. A 2023 study put adaptation costs for all developing countries at around US$215 billion per year up to 2030. Of adaptation-specific funding, 63% came as loans and 36% as grants, and only 66% of committed amounts were paid out.

nature-clim-043.title: Mitigation finance: the bulk of climate money
nature-clim-043.text: Mitigation finance is investment that aims to reduce global greenhouse gas emissions. It dominates, accounting for over 90% of worldwide investment in climate finance. Around 70% of mitigation money has gone to renewable energy; energy efficiency and transport are the other key sectors. Of the estimated US$83.3 billion provided to developing countries in 2020, US$48.6 billion, or 58%, targeted mitigation. The needs are far larger. The 2018 Biennial Assessment put mitigation financing needs for 2020 to 2030 at US$1.7-2.4 trillion per year. The IEA estimates that keeping warming below 2 Celsius needs an average of $3.5 trillion a year of energy-sector investment until 2050.

nature-clim-089.title: The global stocktake: checking the world's progress
nature-clim-089.text: Every five years, the Paris Agreement asks a collective question: how far has the world as a whole got toward its goals? The global stocktake is that review. It links countries' {{ref:nature-clim-071}} to the Paris goals, and its results are meant to feed into their next pledges and raise ambition. It looks at collective progress, so individual countries are not singled out. Its scope was debated. In the end it covers mitigation, adaptation and the means of implementation and support, including finance. It runs in three phases. First comes collecting information, then technical assessment, and finally political messages for policy. The second stocktake begins in November 2026 at COP 31 and concludes two years later at COP 33.

nature-clim-076.title: The enhanced transparency framework: checking what countries do
nature-clim-076.text: Pledges mean little if no one can check them. The enhanced transparency framework, set by Article 13 of {{ref:nature-clim-074}}, is a common system for checking countries' climate action. It covers monitoring, reporting and verifying what they do and the support they give or receive. Parties are legally bound to have their progress toward their NDCs checked by technical expert review. Developed and developing countries alike report every two years and face technical and peer review. It has flexibility in scope, detail and frequency of reporting for countries with less capacity.

nature-clim-079.title: Climate debt: who owes whom for a warming planet
nature-clim-079.text: At the 2009 Copenhagen conference, developing countries led by Bolivia demanded repayment of a debt. Not a loan, but climate debt: what developed countries are said to owe developing ones for the damage caused by their far larger share of climate-changing emissions. The idea is part of the broader concept of {{ref:nature-gov-199}} and was first put forward by NGOs in the 1990s. It has two main parts. {{ref:nature-clim-081}} is the help owed for adapting to climate change. {{ref:nature-clim-080}} is owed for excessive past emissions. Views split along familiar lines. Support comes mainly from developing countries and environmental NGOs, and criticism mostly from developed nations. Critics argue that emissions made before their harm was understood, or by earlier generations, should not create guilt or debts. Others say that even if the idea is ethically sound, its adversarial framing may undermine climate negotiations.

nature-clim-064.title: Action for Climate Empowerment: education and participation
nature-clim-064.text: Since 2015, Action for Climate Empowerment has been the name for the climate convention's work on education, training, public awareness, participation, access to information and cooperation on these. It refers to Article 6 of the 1992 convention text. It calls on governments to run education and awareness programmes, train experts, open up information and encourage the public to take part.

nature-clim-063.title: Why critics say the UN climate process has failed
nature-clim-063.text: Critics argue that the UN climate convention and {{ref:nature-clim-056}} have failed to cut greenhouse gas emissions as intended. With over 190 countries deciding by consensus, small groups of countries can often block progress. Competition gets in the way. In 2010 Japan refused a second Kyoto term because it would face limits that its competitors China, India and Indonesia did not. The convention also failed, mainly under Kyoto, to transfer environmentally sound technologies to developing countries. Historical responsibility for emissions remains contentious in the talks.

nature-clim-065.title: National communications: each country's climate report
nature-clim-065.text: Each country party to the UN climate convention submits a national communication, a report on its climate measures and vulnerabilities. Developed countries must submit one every four years; developing countries should. They are often several hundred pages long, much longer and more detailed than the pledges made under the Paris Agreement. Some least developed countries have not submitted one in 5–15 years, mostly for lack of capacity.

nature-clim-060.title: The Doha Amendment: Kyoto's shrinking second act
nature-clim-060.text: On 8 December 2012 in Doha, countries extended {{ref:nature-clim-056}} with a second commitment period running to 2020. Thirty-seven countries held binding targets, and 2015 was set as the date for a successor agreement. Japan, New Zealand and Russia took on no new targets, and the second period covered only about 11% of global annual emissions. The ending was awkward. The amendment entered into force on 31 December 2020, after 144 states accepted it, on the very day the second period ended.

nature-clim-058.title: Hot air: surplus allowances that cut nothing
nature-clim-058.text: Under Kyoto, Russia, Ukraine and the new EU-12 states got emission targets set above their actual emissions. That left them with a large surplus of allowances, permits to emit, which became known as hot air. These transition economies saw the surplus as 'headroom' to grow their economies. Countries short of allowances could buy them from those with a surplus. But without further commitments that trade would not reduce emissions at all.

nature-clim-059.title: Kyoto's compliance mechanism: penalties with little bite
nature-clim-059.text: {{ref:nature-clim-056}} had a system for checking whether parties met their commitments and penalising those that did not. A party that missed its emissions limit had to make up the difference in the second commitment period, plus an additional 30%. It was also suspended from making transfers under {{ref:nature-pol-253}}. Some doubted the bite. Grubb judged the consequences for non-compliance weak compared with domestic law, and the compliance section was hotly contested in the Marrakesh Accords.

nature-clim-077.title: The 2 degree target: the line the world drew
nature-clim-077.text: Keep global warming below two degrees Celsius above pre-industrial (1850–1900) levels. That is the 2 degree target, an international policy goal. It is a political decision, based on science about the likely consequences of warming, and dates from the 2009 Copenhagen conference. It is central to the Paris Agreement. It is often criticised as too high, since two degrees of warming would have serious effects on people and nature. The IPCC's 2018 special report warned that 2 °C rather than 1.5 °C would worsen extreme weather, sea-ice loss, sea-level rise, coral bleaching and ecosystem loss. The world is not on course to meet it. The UNFCCC predicts a likely 2.1 to 2.9 °C of warming by 2100. An 'overshoot pathway' would pass 2 °C and then bring warming back down late in the century, requiring management over many decades.

nature-clim-075.title: Is the Paris Agreement working
nature-clim-075.text: Most experts say {{ref:nature-clim-074}} is insufficient for its 1.5 °C goal, though some argue it is too early to judge. UNEP said in 2020 that current commitments would likely lead to more than 3 °C of warming by 2100. Studies in Nature found that as of 2017 none of the major industrialised nations was implementing its pledged policies. The other side has numbers too. The stocktake report credits the agreement with a large effect: expected 2100 warming fell from 3.7–4.8 °C in 2010 to 2.4–2.6 °C at COP 27.

nature-clim-072.title: Intended nationally determined contributions: the first drafts
nature-clim-072.text: Before the 2015 Paris Agreement, countries made initial, voluntary and non-binding climate pledges called intended nationally determined contributions. These became their first {{ref:nature-clim-071}}. Parties were asked to publish them at the November 2013 Warsaw climate conference. The term was a compromise between Kyoto's binding 'QELROs' for developed countries and 'NAMAs' for developing ones. Switzerland submitted the first on 27 February 2015. The timing was tight: 85% of surveyed countries said the short time frame was a challenge.

nature-clim-073.title: The ratchet mechanism: tightening pledges every five years
nature-clim-073.text: A ratchet turns only one way. The Paris Agreement's ratchet mechanism is a five-yearly cycle of reporting, review and new pledges designed to raise climate ambition over time. Countries publish progress reports every two years, which undergo technical review. These feed a global stocktake, on an offset five-year cycle, that judges whether all pledges together are enough. Its findings are meant to shape each country's next, more ambitious pledge.

nature-clim-098.title: Pledge and review: from rejected idea to central approach
nature-clim-098.text: Japan first proposed it in 1991. At the first COP in 1995 it was rejected in favour of binding targets, which led to {{ref:nature-clim-056}}. Pledge and review is a way of organising climate action in which each country makes its own pledge, others review its progress, and stronger pledges follow. It is 'bottom-up', unlike legally binding targets imposed 'top-down' by a central body. Revived at Copenhagen in 2009, it drew pledges from countries producing about 80% of global emissions. Kyoto's first targets had covered 25%. By 2015 it was the central approach, though at Paris the pledges were renamed {{ref:nature-clim-071}}. It won because binding targets proved hard to agree and impossible to enforce on powerful nations. Opinion remains divided. Critics called it 'hedge and retreat' or 'second best', while others called it an essential pillar of mitigation.

nature-clim-087.title: The Glasgow Climate Pact: phasing down coal
nature-clim-087.text: On 13 November 2021, the COP26 conference in Glasgow produced the first climate agreement explicitly planning to reduce unabated coal use. Late in the talks, a pledge to 'phase out' coal became 'phase down', at the urging of coal-reliant countries such as India and China. Countries agreed to revisit their emission plans in 2022 to keep the 1.5 °C target within reach, and committed to climate finance for developing countries. Around the summit, more than 140 countries pledged net-zero emissions and more than 100 pledged to reverse deforestation by 2030.
